segments.text: Daniel hurried down the same street every morning. He knew its cracks, its corners, and exactly how long his journey took.
Today, an older man named Eli stood beside the bench. When his paper bag slipped, bread scattered across the pavement.
Daniel saw it happen. He shortened his stride, then looked away. Someone else would stop. Surely someone else had more time.
But after a few steps, the street grew quiet. Behind him, Eli lowered himself carefully, reaching for bread just beyond his fingers.
Daniel stopped beside the bench. He remembered words he had heard many times, but had not yet practiced that morning.
Jesus said, “Thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself.” Matthew twenty-two, verse thirty-nine. The words asked something simple of him now.
Daniel turned around. He could not change the whole world before breakfast. But he could return to the person he had passed.
He approached slowly and asked if Eli would like a hand. Eli nodded. Daniel knelt and gathered the scattered loaves.
Some bread was still wrapped. One piece had fallen loose. Daniel set that piece aside instead of putting it back.
Together, they opened the bag. Eli steadied it while Daniel placed the wrapped bread inside. Neither needed to hurry now.
Daniel offered to carry the bag. Eli accepted, then pointed down the street. They began walking together, at Eli’s pace.
The journey took longer than Daniel had planned. Yet for once, he noticed the warmth of the morning along the way.
Loving a neighbour had not required a grand speech. It had begun with noticing, turning back, and offering help without taking over.
That morning, Daniel arrived late. But he understood something he had almost walked past: love becomes visible in the next kind thing we do.
